list.listitem: The United States Preventative Task Force (USPTF) recommends screening everyone with risk factors for contracting Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) and anyone requesting HIV testing annually, and all adults and adolescents age 15 to 65 years at least once. Younger adolescents and older adults who are at increased risk of infection should also be screened. All pregnant persons should be screened for HIV. ACenter for Disease Control (CDC) recommends screening ages 15 to 65 if sexually active, using “opt out testing” - offering testing to all patients and allowing them to “opt out” of testing. A
Primary HIV infection usually presents with an influenza-like illness within 2 to 4 weeks of exposure. Presentation commonly includes fever, rash, and lymphadenopathy. C

Consider the risk of advancement to Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome (AIDS), risk of developing non-AIDS diseases, medical comorbidities, patient readiness, and funding source for consistency of access when initiating treatment. C
Primary care responsibilities include immunizations, preventative screenings, contraception, family planning discussion and management of comorbidities. C

Offer therapy with antiretroviral medications (ARV) to all HIV positive patients, regardless of CD4 numbers, and with increased urgency in patients with CD4 below 350c/dl, renal insufficiency, hepatitis B or C, malignancy, or opportunistic infections regardless of CD4 count. A

Refer to Infectious Disease, or if comfortable with ARV management, begin therapy with a three or four drug antiretroviral regimen in all patients. Benefit is greater with lower CD4 counts and comorbidities such as hepatitis C coinfection, renal failure, hepatitis B and opportunistic infections (OI). Refer to guidelines from the Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS) Panel and International Antiviral Society – USA (IAS-USA) panel (Table 2). A

Monitor plasma HIV-1 RNA levels within ARV guidelines after initiation or change in medication regimen , along with renal and hepatic function panels depending on choice of ARV, then in 8 to 12 weeks until suppression occurs. Assess HIV-1 RNA levels quarterly after confirmed suppression and twice a year after a sustained CD4 cell count greater than 350 cells/μL occurs with a suppressed viral load for 2 years. After two years of sustained undetectable viral load, HIV specific labs can be drawn every six months. A

Clinical trials have shown that using effective antiretroviral therapy (ART) to consistently suppress plasma HIV RNA levels to <200 copies/mL prevents transmission of HIV to sexual partners. When ART is used to prevent HIV transmission, this strategy is called treatment as prevention (TasP), commonly known as Undetectable = Untransmittable or U=U. A
Offer PrEP to partners that are serodisconcordant, engaging in risk behaviour or at risk to contract HIV. A
Consider switch therapy for well-controlled patients to single tablet or injectable therapy. B

background.definition: Human immunodeficiency virus, HIV, is a retrovirus that attacks and destroys CD4+ T helper cells. The helper cells participate in cell-mediated immunity. As their numbers decrease, the patient is prone to a variety of opportunistic infections and malignancies. There are two types of HIV: HIV-1 and HIV-2. HIV-1 is more common and is found worldwide. HIV-2 is found predominantly in West Africa and progression is slower than HIV-1. (Date: July 24, 1995 National Institutes of Health (NIH)).

list.listitem: HIV incidence declined 8% from 2015 to 2019. In 2019, the estimated number of new HIV infections in the U.S. was 34,800 and the rate was 12.6 (per 100,000 people). By age group, the annual number of HIV infections in 2019, compared with 2015, decreased among persons aged 13–24 and persons aged 45-54, but remained stable among all other age groups.

By HIV transmission category, the annual number of HIV infections in 2019, compared with 2015, decreased among males with transmission attributed to male-to-male sexual contact, but remained stable among all other transmission categories. In 2019, the largest percentages of HIV infections were attributed to male-to-male sexual contact (66% overall and 81% among males.)In 2014 to 2018, the number of people receiving an HIV diagnosis in the US decreased. In the United States and territories, the overall rate in 2018 was 11.5; among adults and adolescents the rate was 13.6. From 2014 through 2018, by region, the rate of diagnoses of HIV infection in all regions decreased. In 2018, the rates were 15.6 in the South, 9.9 in the Northeast, 9.7 in the West, and 7.2 in the Midwest.

In 2019, the rate was highest for persons aged 25-34, followed by the rate for persons aged 35-44. By race/ethnicity, the annual number of HIV infections in 2019, compared with 2015, decreased among persons of multiple races, but remained stable for persons of all other races/ethnicities. In 2019, the highest rate was for Blacks/African American persons, followed by Hispanic/Latino persons and persons of multiple races. By sex at birth, the annual number of new HIV infections in 2019, as compared to 2015, decreased among males, but remained stable among females. In 2019, the rate for males was 5 times the rate for females .Among 245,154 females living with diagnosed HIV infection in 2018, 58% were Black/African American, 20% were Hispanic/Latino, 16% were White, 5% were females of multiple races, and 1% were Asian. Less than 1% each were American Indian/Alaska Native and Native Hawaiian/other Pacific Islander.
For patients on ARV, perinatal transmission and heterosexual transmission is minimal, often without ARV during pregnancy but during delivery or third trimester.
In 2020, 30,635 people received an HIV diagnosis in the United States and dependent areas. The number of new diagnoses decreased 8% from 2016 to 2019.

In 2020, male-to-male sexual contactd accounted for 68% of all new HIV diagnoses in the United States and dependent areas. In the same year, heterosexual contact accounted for 22% of all HIV diagnoses.
The South has the highest number of people living with HIV, but if population size is taken into account, the Northeast has the highest rate of people living with HIV.
HIV is transmitted via sexual intercourse, exposure to contaminated blood or body fluids, or through perinatal transmission.

High-risk exposure includes receptive anal intercourse and the use of shared needles or syringes among injection drug users. Medium-risk exposure includes vaginal intercourse or intercourse with a partner with uncontrolled HIV. Low-risk exposure involves sex with partners who have controlled HIV or individuals who are taking PrEP and/or consistent condom usage.

HIV infects host CD4 T lymphocytes by attachment and invasion. Once inside, HIV uses reverse transcriptase to convert its viral RNA into DNA and HIV integrase to combine its DNA with the host's DNA. This is then transcribed into viral RNA and translated into HIV proteins. These proteins become virions that become infectious when cleaved by HIV protease.
In the process, HIV kills the host's CD4 T lymphocytes, the host becomes immunologically compromised, and eventually succumbs to a myriad of diseases.
ARV works in several locations, depending on the medication class, ultimately reducing the HIV virus's ability to replicate.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: For HIV negative anal receptive intercourse with HIV positive without using condoms or taking meds to prevent or treat HIV
HIV negative vaginal intercourse with above partners
Individuals whose past or present sexual partners include injection drug users with shared needles
History of blood transfusion between 1978 and 1985

list.listitem: Screen everyone with risk factors for HIV, as well as anyone requesting HIV testing. Suggest screening to patients as part of routine health maintenance. A

As of 2019, the USPSTF recommends screening all adults and adolescents age 15 to 65 years at least once, and to screen younger and older patients if they are at increased risk. Screening should be repeated for patients with ongoing increased risk. A

HIV prevention consists of a comprehensive plan, including viral control to suppress plasma HIV RNA levels to <200 copies/mL for persons living with HIV, Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis (PrEP), condom usage and behavioral intervention. A
Consistent use of condoms and viral control of HIV reduces the risk of HIV infection. A
Social determinants of health such as food security, access, housing and transportation affect HIV viral control.
The USPSTF recommends screening all adolescents and adults at increased risk for HIV infection. Screening should be repeated for persons with ongoing risk factors for infection.
An individual is considered to have increased risk if he or she reports one or more individual risk factors or receives health care in a high prevalence area or high-risk clinical setting in the US.

Anyone requesting HIV screening should be screened. Individuals may be considered high risk for HIV if requesting testing without known high risk behavior as it may include persons not willing to divulge high risk behaviors.

listitem.strong: Screening for other conditions in persons living with HIV (PLWH)

list.listitem: At initial HIV care visit, providers should test all sexually active persons with HIV infection for curable STDs (e.g., syphilis, gonorrhea, and chlamydia), and perform testing at least annually during HIV care.
Herpes simplex virus screening is recommended at entry to care using serum testing.
Patients should be tested for latent cytomegalovirus infection (CMV) with an anti-CMV IgG upon initiation of care, with risk assessment (higher for MSM and injection drug users).
All patients should be screened for syphilis upon initiation of care and periodically thereafter, depending on risk. Intervals suggested are annually or every 6 months.

Patients should receive hepatitis C screening at initial evaluation and then annually in MSM with HIV, IV drug users or other risk factors. Hepatitis C viral RNA should be ordered on all those with a positive hepatitis C antibody test to assess for active disease. Hepatitis C treatment should be offered to all HIV positive individuals after cirrhosis staging with cure as goal.

Annual testing for Neisseria gonorrhea and Chlamydia trachomatis is recommended for individuals who are sexually active. Use nucleic acid testing to test all relevant orifices, including pharynx and anus.

T. vaginalis infection is associated with two- to threefold increased risk for HIV acquisition. Among women with HIV infection, T. vaginalis infection is associated with increased risk for PID. Routine annual screening of asymptomatic women with HIV infection for T. vaginalis is recommended because of the adverse events associated with asymptomatic trichomoniasis and HIV infection. Screen any woman presenting with vaginal discharge for T. vaginalis.

Digital rectal exam for palpable condyloma is recommended annually for all individuals engaging in ano-receptive intercourse. Anal pap smears should be considered in some areas of the US, depending on funding and specialist support.In a non-blinded randomized controlled trial of 10,723 persons living with HIV, 41.5% screened positive for high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions (HSIL) using liquid-based anal cytology and high-resolution anoscopy. Compared to surveillance, immediate treatment decreased anal cancer at 28 months by 0.9% (0.9% vs 1.8%, NNT 111)

As patients with HIV have a higher risk for cervical cancer, PAP smear is recommended annually using liquid cytology and reflex testing per Bethesda guidelines for HIV positive women and transgender individuals.
Ophthalmological screening for CMV retinitis is recommended annually in individuals with CD4 <200.
Dental exam, including oral cavity exam is recommended at least annually for decay, gingivitis, oral malignancy screening and hygiene
HIV prevention consists of a comprehensive plan, including viral control for persons living with HIV, PrEP, condom usage and behavioral intervention.

Consistent use of condoms results in 80% reduction in new cases of HIV in heterosexuals. Circumcision was found to reduce the risk of HIV infection in heterosexual men with reduced viral control in areas of high prevalence such as Sub Saharan Africa. More investigation is needed regarding the role of circumcision in HIV prevention in men who have sex with other men.
Complete adherence to universal precautions for healthcare workers is recommended.

For patients with HIV and helper T cells (CD4) >200, immunizations are suggested. Recommended immunizations for all HIV positive adults include H influenza type B, hepatitis A and B, human papilloma virus, pneumonia, zoster, meningococcal, Influenza and varicella. It is not recommended to administer anthrax, smallpox, or other live attenuated vaccines without data. Criteria should be reviewed for each vaccination and individual patient stage of HIV infectionCovid vaccination and 90 day refills are recommended during the worldwide SARS-COV pandemic ( CDC)
Routine preventative care and screening is recommended for Persons Living With HIV (PLWH).

Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) for preventing HIV in HIV-uninfected high-risk patients uses tenofovir disoproxil fumarate and emtricitabine for both MSM and heterosexual women. Tenofovir alafenamide and emtricitabine have also been studied as effective for PrEP usage in MSM; this reduced the relative risk of new HIV infection by up to 90%. In sero-disconcordant couples where the HIV positive individual has an undetectable viral load, risk of transmitting the HIV virus is minimal. PrEP should be taken daily, and HIV and sexually transmitted infection (STI) screening completed at regular intervals for HIV negative partners, for the duration of risk exposure. An injectable form of cabotegravir (Apretude) has been FDA approved in December 2021 based on the results from two, international phase IIb/III multicenter, randomized, double-blind, active-controlled trials.

listitem.strong: Other immunizations for persons living with HIV (PLWH)

list.listitem: PLWH who have CD4 counts lower than 200 cells/mm3 or certain symptoms of HIV should not get live, attenuated vaccines. Routine immunizations at these lower levels of immunity will also result in less effective vaccine, so vaccinations should be deferred until CD4 levels have risen to over 200, irrespective of viral load.
Influenza vaccination is recommended for CD4 counts above 50. Pneumonia vaccines (PCV 13) may also be given at CD4 counts of 100.

HIV infected patients should be screened for hepatitis B and hepatitis A, and if nonimmune, immunize. HBsAb should be repeated 1 to 2 months or at the next scheduled visit after the third vaccine was given to assess for immunogenicity. A second series of vaccine is recommended for those whose HBsAb levels are negative or <10 IU/mL after vaccine series. Hepatitis A total or IgG antibody should be repeated 1 to 2 months or at the next scheduled visit after the second vaccine to assess for immunogenicity. A repeat vaccine series is recommended in those who remain seronegative.

HPV vaccination is recommended for all females aged 9 to 26 years and all males aged 9 to 21 years. Males aged 22 to 26 years should also be vaccinated if not vaccinated at younger ages. Many state Medicaid programs, commercial insurance carriers, and Ryan White will cover HPV vaccination for older individuals.
Consider shingles vaccine in patients >age 60 with varicella immunity and CD4 ≥200 cells/mm.

All patients with a CD4 >200 should receive both pneumococcal 13-valent conjugate vaccine, and 23-valent polysaccharide vaccine. PCV13 should be administered first followed by PPV23 in 8 or more weeks. A booster dose of PCV23 should be given 5 years after the first PPV 23. If a patient has previously received PPV23, immunization with PCV13 should be delayed by 1 year.
All PLWH should receive Tdap once regardless of the time since their most recent Td booster.
Covid vaccination and boosters are recommended during the Sars-CoV pandemic.
Monkeypox vaccination is recommended for all MSM who are PLWH.

listitem.strong: Antiretroviral Therapy to Prevent Sexual Transmission of HIV (Treatment as Prevention TaSP)

list.listitem: Clinical trials have shown that using effective antiretroviral therapy (ART) to consistently suppress plasma HIV RNA levels to <200 copies/mL prevents transmission of HIV to sexual partners. When ART is used to prevent HIV transmission, this strategy is called treatment as prevention (TasP), commonly known as Undetectable = Untransmittable or U=U.

The Panel on Antiretroviral Guidelines for Adults and Adolescents has added a new section to help providers integrate TasP into their clinical practice. The key recommendations include providers informing persons with HIV that maintaining HIV RNA levels <200 copies/mL with ART prevents HIV transmission to sexual partners.

Persons starting ART should use another form of prevention with sexual partners for at least the first 6 months of treatment and until an HIV RNA level of <200 copies/mL has been documented. Many experts recommend confirming sustained suppression before assuming that there is no risk of sexual HIV transmission.

Persons with HIV who rely on ART for prevention need to maintain high levels of ART adherence. They should be informed that transmission is possible during periods of poor adherence or treatment interruption. Providers should inform patients that maintaining an HIV RNA level of <200 copies/mL does not prevent acquisition or transmission of other sexually transmitted infections.

In a review of 8 studies involving 7762 serodiscordant couples from 25 countries, researchers found that when the HIV-positive partner's viral load was less than 200 copies per mL, there was no sexual transmission of HIV. Additionally, the majority of transmissions occurred when viral loads exceeded 10,000 copies per mL, with only 2 cases of transmission at viral loads under 1000 copies per mL

Advise safe sexual practices in persons with HIV, even if their partner is also infected with the virus. HIV superinfection with other genotypes of HIV virus is found to have an incidence of 5% per year. Superinfection with HIV wild-type may lead to masking of drug-resistant strain, resulting in ineffective therapy and poor prognosis.

Non-occupational PEP preferred regimens: tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (tenofovir DF or TDF) (300 mg) with emtricitabine (200 mg) once daily plus raltegravir (RAL) 400 mg twice daily or dolutegravir (DTG) 50 mg daily.

Occupational needlestick or fluid post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) protocols no longer recommend that the severity of exposure be used to determine the number of drugs to be offered in an HIV PEP regimen. Routine recommendation for all occupational exposures to HIV involves regimens of three (or more) antiretroviral drugs.

All PEP regimens should be started within 72 hours and duration of treatment should last for 4 weeks. The exposed individual should undergo testing and treatment counseling with discussion of risks of seroconversion, HIV testing, and a medical evaluation. HIV testing is recommended at 6 weeks, 12 weeks, and 6 months.
Examples of recommended PEP regimens include: Those consisting of a dual NRTI backbone plus an INSTI A PI (boosted with ritonavir) A NNRTI.PEP should begin as soon as possible,

The suggested regimen includes emtricitabine (FTC) plus TDF, (these two agents may be dispensed as Truvada, a fixed-dose combination tablet) plus raltegravir (RAL) as HIV PEP for occupational exposures to HIV. This regimen is tolerable, potent, and conveniently administered, and it has been associated with minimal drug interactions.
Obtain a thorough risk and sexual history and offer options when available to protect individuals engaging in high risk behaviors. C
Primary HIV infection usually presents with an influenza-like illness within 2 to 4 weeks of exposure. C
To make the diagnosis of HIV, send blood sample for HIV antibody detection. Alternatively, testing of oral secretions or urine can be performed to make a rapid diagnosis. A
Offer PrEP and serial/interval testing every 6 months or annually to patients at risk for HIV infection.
There are three types of HIV diagnostic tests: nucleic acid tests (NAT), antigen/antibody tests, and antibody tests ().

NATs look for HIV virus in the blood. This test is not used for HIV screening unless the person recently had a high-risk exposure or a possible exposure with early symptoms of Acute HIV infection (HIV RNA, HIV viral load).

Antigen/antibody tests for HIV antibodies and antigens. The antigen p24 is produced even before antibodies develop and useful in acute HIV. Tests that detect both antigen and antibodies are recommended for testing. Rapid antigen/antibody testing is available.
Antibody tests detect the presence of antibodies, proteins that a person's body makes against HIV, not HIV itself. Most rapid tests and home tests are antibody tests.
Stages of HIV infection are summarized below:
Laboratory criteria met without information on CD4 cell count or percentage or AIDS defining illness.
CD4 often >1500
Within 2 to 4 weeks after infection with HIV.
Flu-like illness, fever, rash, lymphadenopathy, myalgia
Associated with high viral replication and increased infectivity
Beginning ARV in this period is recommended and retains immunity.
Sometimes called asymptomatic HIV infection or chronic HIV infection
HIV is still replicating but reproduces at very low levels
If left untreated, usually progresses to AIDS in 8 to 10 years, occasionally less
Patients taking ARV consistently may be in this stage for several decades or lifelong.
AIDS is the most severe phase of HIV infection, often final if untreated
Can be reversed with ARV and treatment of opportunistic infections, as well as comorbidities such as Hep C or malignancy.
Begin prophylaxis for opportunistic infections in this phase.

Acute retroviral syndrome, also termed primary HIV infection, develops within 2 to 4 weeks of infection in up to 90% of individuals. Primary HIV infection usually presents as an influenza-like illness. Fever and rash are best clinical predictors of possible primary HIV infection, followed by oral ulcers, pharyngitis and weight loss.

The 10% who do not experience primary HIV infection or who remained undiagnosed after will come to medical attention through STD screenings or at the point of manifestation of AIDS defining/opportunistic diseases or infections.

The pre-test probability of an acute retroviral syndrome based on patient risk factors is an important part of the decision to pursue further testing. Even otherwise low-risk patients may become infected.

When individuals with sexually transmitted infections (STI) are exposed to HIV through sexual contact, they are at least 2 to 5 times more likely to acquire HIV than their uninfected counterparts. Also, individuals who are positive for HIV and another sexually transmitted disease are more likely to transmit HIV through sexual contact. If patients present with STI, screening for HIV is recommended.
Acute presentations suggesting AIDS include shortness of breath with fever, oral thrush, acute neurologic findings, new seizure, or new onset lymphadenopathy.
4th generation testing is recommended.

Quantitative RNA testing/ viral load is recommended at diagnosis and subsequently to monitor progression of disease and response to treatment. Testing for genotype to assess resistance at the time of treatment initiation is also recommended.

Determine baseline renal function prior to initiation of therapy, and screen for coinfection with mycobacterium tuberculosis at diagnosis, hepatitis B, hepatitis C, syphilis, and toxoplasmosis exposure is also recommended.

If concerned that the patient may have an AIDS-defining illness, utilize diagnostic testing for individual infections, such as induced sputum for pneumocystis pneumonia, tuberculin skin testing for mycobacterium, or stool testing for cryptosporidium.
For patients beginning highly active antiretroviral therapy, the likelihood of progression can be predicted by a validated clinical rule.

Create a “safe space” during the clinical interview, routinely exploring sexual history without judgement and screening for high risk behaviors in all patients. Maintain clinical inquiry for acute retroviral syndrome or primary HIV infection in patients with influenza-like illness, especially if accompanied by rash, oral ulcers, pharyngitis, and weight loss.

Standard testing in HIV includes 4th generation ag/ab HIV serum testing with p24 evaluation. If rapid testing from oral or other cellular testing is obtained, confirmation with serum testing is recommended.
Begin therapy with a three-drug continuous antiretroviral regimen in all patients with CD4 cell count less than 350/μL.

Routinely obtain sexual history and assess for high risk behaviors. Approach the patient with sensitivity and do not assume consent has occurred with high risk activity. Consider acute retroviral syndrome or primary HIV infection in patients with influenza-like illness, especially if accompanied by rash, oral ulcers, pharyngitis, and weight loss.
Standard testing in HIV includes HIV serology with enzyme immunoassay and confirmation with western blot or immunofluorescent assay (IFA).
Refer to Treatment section for details on drug therapy and other treatments.
Treatment should be advocated for all coinfections such as hepatitis C, syphilis or STI as treatment will improve outcomes of mortality related to HIV.

Consider the risk of advancement to AIDS, risk of developing non-AIDS diseases, present comorbidities, and patient's readiness when initiating treatment. C Consider antiretroviral therapy to all patients with HIV disease; benefit is greater in those with lower CD4 counts, evidence of AIDS defining condition, co-infection with hepatitis, chronic renal disease and higher viral loads. A

A two, three or four drug antiretroviral regimen is recommended—see Table 2 for recommendations from the International Antiviral Society USA Panel, 39 on initial treatment and also refer to DHHS HIV Guidelines. A
Treat opportunistic infections when they occur. If they occur during ART, consider therapy modification. A
Conduct resistance testing in all cases of therapy failure. A

Recommendations regarding initial ARV therapy from the International Antiviral Society – USA (IAS-USA) Panel for Treatment are patient specific, and the following should be considered: the risk of advancement to AIDS, risk of developing non-AIDS diseases, comorbidities (e.g., hepatitis, cardiovascular disease, cancer, and renal disease), and patient readiness to engage in treatment.

The most recent guidelines recommend initiating ARV therapy in all individuals infected with HIV, recognizing that the benefit and strength of evidence is greatest for those with pretreatment CD4 levels <350 cells/μL, followed by those with levels of 350-500 cells/μL, and then those with CD4 counts >500 cells/μL. Appropriate counseling regarding risks and benefits is recommended before initiating therapy.

Those more likely to benefit include pregnant patients, those with an AIDS defining condition, those coinfected with hepatitis B or C, and those with higher viral loads (>100,000 copies/mL). Genotypic/resistance testing is recommended in the following clinical situations: before initiating treatment in treatment-naive patients with chronic or primary HIV, in treatment failure while patient is still taking the failed medication, and when initiating treatment in pregnant mothers.
Primary HIV infection is an indication to initiate antiretroviral therapy.
Selection of medications (Table 2).

There are six classes of ARV, including nucleoside/nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs), non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTIs), protease inhibitors (PIs), a fusion inhibitor (FI), a CCR5 antagonist, and integrase strand transfer inhibitors (INSTIs). In addition, ritonavir (RTV or r) and cobicistat (COBI or c) are used solely as pharmacokinetic (PK) boosters to improve the pharmacokinetic profiles of some ARV drugs (e.g., PIs and the INSTI elvitegravir (EVG). When selecting a treatment regimen, consider the patient's comorbidities, drug interactions, contraceptive needs, anticipated tolerability, acceptable pill burden and dosing frequency. Always discuss the short and long term medication adverse events, resources for payment and all other provider/patient barriers.

In developed countries, up to 20% of transmitted HIV is a resistant strain. Conduct resistance testing before initiation of therapy. If necessary, begin therapy while awaiting results (takes about 2 weeks) and modify therapy as indicated.
The Panel on Antiretroviral Guidelines for Adults and Adolescents classifies the following regimens as recommended initial regimens for most people with HIV :

listitem.strong: For people without a history of using cabotegravir-LA as PrEP:

listitem.em: An integrase strand transfer inhibitors (INSTI) plus two nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs):

list.listitem: Bictegravir/tenofovir alafenamide/emtricitabine
Dolutegravir/abacavir/lamivudine—only for individuals who are HLA-B*5701 negative and without chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) coinfection
Dolutegravir plus (emtricitabine or lamivudine) plus (tenofovir alafenamide or tenofovir disoproxil fumarate)

Dolutegravir/lamivudine, except for individuals with HIV RNA >500,000 copies/mL, HBV co-infection, or in whom ART is to be started before the results of HIV genotypic resistance testing for reverse transcriptase or HBV testing are available.

listitem.strong: For people with HIV and a history of using CAB-LA

list.listitem: INSTI genotypic resistance testing should be done before the start of antiretroviral therapy. If treatment is begun prior to results of genotypic testing, the following regimen is recommended:
Boosted darunavir plus (alafenamide or tenofovir disoproxil fumarate) plus (emtricitabine or lamivudine)—pending the results of the genotype test.

A trial randomized 566 persons with HIV to long-acting injectable therapy with cabotegravir plus rilpivirine was equivalent to oral therapy with dolutegravir-abacavir-lamivudine for the outcome of maintaining HIV-1 suppression. A second very similar trial in the same issue of the journal with 616 patients had similar results.

A randomized trial concluded that adding fostemsavir, an HIV-1 attachment inhibitor, reduces viral RNA levels in patients with multi-drug resistant HIV. This regimen now has FDA aprroval for switch once viral control has been achieved.
Review treatment history and resistance testing results prior to changing medications. Refer to the most recent DHHS guidelines for the most recent recommendations.

The goal of changing medication is to maintain the potency of the treatment regimen. Reasons for changing medications include decreasing toxicity, avoiding adverse drug interactions, and improving convenience and patient compliance. Monitor for persistent adverse effects that may lead to patient noncompliance
In women who are planning pregnancy or have fertility concerns, consider CCR5 antagonist based on resistance testing results and available options.

A randomized trial found that episodic ARV therapy based on CD4+ cell count significantly increased the risk of death or opportunistic diseases when compared with continuous therapy. Due to increased likelihood of developing resistance, it is not the suggested regimen.
Opioids—some ARV, primarily NNRTI's and PI's will increase elimination half-life of opioid, especially methadone, resulting in decreased effectiveness of previously tolerated doses.

Due to the inhibition of hepatic cytochrome P450 3A4 isozyme, HIV protease inhibitors can result in significant drug-drug interactions. One noteworthy interaction is between protease inhibitors and inhaled or intranasal corticosteroids. This interaction can result in adrenal insufficiency, iatrogenic Cushing's syndrome, as well as hypertension, osteoporosis, and decreased CD4+ cell count. Certain nutritional supplements can interfere with absorption of some ARVs (integrase inhibitors and PI’s): Polyvalent cations (iron, calcium, magnesium, aluminum in Mylanta, selenium) and the herbal preparation St John's Wort.
Exercise caution when using chronic NSAIDS and diuretics and some ARV has increased risk of renal insufficiency (tenofovir d, Cobicistat indirectly).
Practice judicious avoidance of PPI/H2 blockers as they interfere with absorption of some ARVs as they require stomach acid for absorption (Complera, Odefsey, Reyataz, Juluca, Edurant).

Lipid lowering medication: simvastatin and mevacor are contraindicated owing to high risk of myalgias and rhabdomyolysis. Rosuvastatin, atorvastatin and pravastatin are suitable but initiate at lower doses as ARV may boost level of the statin, seen especially with protease inhibitors and INSTI. No significant interactions with zetia, omega 3, or niacin have been observed.
Some ARVs have increased risk of renal insufficiency and lactic acidosis (tenofovir d).
Some ARVs can increase levels of metformin. The maximum recommended dose of metformin if given with dolutegravir or biktegravir is 1 gram.
Anti-platelet and anti-coagulants show possible increased or decreased effect if given with specific ARVs; Eliquis, Pradaxa, Savaysa and warfarin are acceptable.

Investigations have associated some of the antiretrovirals with QT prolongation, which may result in additive cardiotoxicity in patients also receiving amiodarone; signs of toxicity can be unmasked by EKG and clinical history.
Use caution with anticonvulsant and psychiatric medications, especially with sedatives and antipsychotics prescribed with dolutegravir and tenofovir alafenamide.

Pharmacokinetic interactions between ARV drugs and hormonal contraceptives can reduce contraceptive efficacy. However, there are limited clinical data regarding drug interactions between ARVs and hormonal contraceptives and the clinical implications of these interactions are unclear. The magnitudes of changes in drug levels that may reduce contraceptive efficacy or increase adverse effects are unknown.

Combined oral contraceptives (COCs): several PIs, EFV, and elvitegravir/cobicistat (EVG/c)-based regimens have drug interactions with COCs. Interactions include either a decrease or an increase in blood levels of ethinyl estradiol, norethindrone, or norgestimate, which potentially decreases contraceptive efficacy or increases estrogen- or progestin-related adverse effects (e.g., thromboembolism). EFV can decrease etonogestrel bioavailability and plasma progestin concentrations of COCs containing ethinyl estradiol and norgestimate. Several PI/r and EVG/c decrease oral contraceptive estradiol levels. Several PK studies have shown that ETR, RPV, and NVP use did not significantly affect estradiol or progestin levels in women with HIV using COCs.

Injectable contraceptives: small studies of women with HIV receiving injectable depot-medroxyprogesterone acetate (DMPA) while on ART showed no significant interactions between DMPA and EFV, lopinavir/ritonavir (LPV/r), NVP, nelfinavir (NFV), or NRTI drugs.

Intrauterine devices (IUDs) appear to be a safe and effective contraceptive option for women with HIV.47-49 Although studies have focused primarily on nonhormone-containing IUDs, several small studies have found that levonorgestrel-releasing IUDs are also safe and not associated with increased genital tract shedding of HIV.

Contraceptive implants: contraceptive failure of the etonogestrel implant in women on EFV-based therapy has been reported. Studies of women with levonorgestrel- and etonogestrel-releasing implants reported that participants receiving EFV-based ART had decreased bioavailability of levonorgestrel and etonogestrel. These studies did not identify any change in hormone concentrations when the implants were used in women taking NVP40 or LPV/r. Similarly, two retrospective cohort evaluations conducted in Swaziland and Kenya showed an increased risk of contraceptive failure in women using contraceptive implants and receiving EFV.

Concerns about interactions between oral or implantable hormonal contraceptives and ARVs should not prevent clinicians from prescribing hormonal contraceptives for women on ART who prefer this contraceptive method. However, an alternative or additional effective contraceptive method is recommended when there are significant drug interactions between hormonal contraceptives and oral contraceptives; a method that involves no estrogens.
Many hepatitis C medications interact with ARV. Consult with an infectious disease and/or hepatology specialist if treating a patient with coinfection.
Aerobic and resistance exercise have independent and combined positive effects on various indicators of mental health in people living with HIV.
Psychiatric disorders and substance abuse are highly comorbid with HIV infection.
Mental health problems can stem from or from the stigma, stress and socio-economic challenges presented by living with HIV/AIDS.

Depression and substance use disorders are known to increase the risk of behaviors that promote HIV transmission, such as risky sexual activity and injecting drug-use. PLWH should be routinely screened for depression, anxiety, and other mood disorders. Use motivational interviewing and shared decision making to collaboratively discuss functional and treatment goals, and barriers to care.Integrating HIV and mental health services may be linked to improved patient and service delivery outcomes in diverse settings.
Substance use does not prohibit treatment with ARV, but certain illicit substances such as cocaine are potentiated by ARV such as ritonavir.
Adherence and improved outcomes to HIV treatment regimens are directly influenced by social support and mental health.
Patient preferences around confidentiality, revealing status to partners or family and individuals with decision making capacity for patient should be discussed.
There is strong evidence that risk of interpersonal violence (IPV) is elevated in PLWH, and emerging evidence links IPV and/or HIV to a higher likelihood of experiencing mental health problems.

Ask PLWH about their reproductive goals and create a treatment plan that respects said goals, if possible. Long-Acting Reproductive Control is recommended for women living with HIV on ART who prefer this contraceptive method. However, an alternative or additional effective contraceptive method is recommended when there are significant drug interactions between hormonal contraceptives and oral contraceptives; use a method that involves no estrogens.

All women of reproductive age should be engaged in discussion around reproductive choices, including preservation or long term control of fertility. Oral contraceptives are not preferred. Ideally, patients received injectable depot progesterone, Long Acting Reproductive Control (LARC) such as subdermal implantable devices or intrauterine contraceptive devices.

Male patients should also participate in this discussion, including long terms plans for reproductive control and HIV prevention for serodisconcordant partners. Sperm washing and banking, along with reproductive assistance is not available in most of the United States for PLWH.

Encourage smoking cessation. The effect of medical marijuana for HIV/AIDS patients experiencing weight loss and poor appetite is unclear, and there is insufficient data to justify its use for this purpose.

Specific nutritional interventions focusing on protein supplements or daily supplementation with spirulina (a cyanobacterium that can be consumed by humans), did not alter the risk of death in malnourished ART naïve HIV-infected patients; nor did these interventions alter clinical or immunological outcomes among HIV-infected adults and children.
In several randomized controlled trials, selenium supplementation has reduced hospitalizations and diarrheal morbidity, and improved CD4 cell counts, but the evidence remains mixed.

In a study involving 7769 adults aged 40 to 75 years with HIV infection and on antiretroviral therapy, patients were randomized to receive either pitavastatin or placebo, with pitavastatin chosen for its lack of interaction with antiretrovirals. The study found a significant reduction in cardiovascular events in the pitavastatin group compared to placebo, with a hazard ratio of 0.65 and a number needed to treat of 82 over 5 years to prevent one event, while serious adverse events were rare and similar between groups.

In a study of 501 men who have sex with men and transgender women, either on PrEP or living with HIV, participants were randomized to receive doxycycline post-exposure prophylaxis after condomless sexual encounters. The intervention group showed a significant reduction in sexually transmitted infections (STIs) at a quarterly visit, with a number needed to treat of 5, but there was an indication of increased doxycycline resistance, necessitating further research on resistance implications.

listitem.strong: Treatment of COVID-19 in patients with HIV

list.listitem: Individuals aged >60 years and those with diabetes, hypertension, cardiovascular disease, pulmonary disease, or obesity are at highest risk of life-threatening COVID-19. The limited data currently available do not indicate that the disease course of COVID-19 in persons with HIV differs from that in persons without HIV. Before the advent of effective combination antiretroviral therapy (ART), advanced HIV infection (i.e., CD4 cell count <200/mm3) was a risk factor for complications of other respiratory infections. Whether this is also true for COVID-19 is yet unknown.

Some PLWH have other comorbidities (e.g., cardiovascular disease, lung disease) that increase the risk for a more severe course of COVID-19 illness. Chronic smokers are also at risk of more severe disease. Until more is known, additional caution for all persons with HIV, especially those with advanced HIV or poorly controlled HIV, is warranted. Influenza and pneumococcal vaccinations should be kept up to date. Persons with HIV should follow all applicable recommendations to prevent COVID-19, such as social distancing and proper hand hygiene.

Ideally maintain a 90-day supply of ARV drugs and other medications. Mail order or contactless delivery should be attempted at every opportunity. Consider delaying ARV switch if possible, until a time when follow up and medication monitoring can resume normal schedules. Many drugs, including some ARV agents (e.g., lopinavir/ritonavir, boosted darunavir, tenofovir disoproxil fumarate/emtricitabine), are being evaluated in clinical trials or are prescribed for off label use for the treatment or prevention of COVID-19. Persons with HIV should not switch their ARV regimens or add ARV drugs to their regimens for the purpose of preventing or treating SARS-CoV-2 infection.

Persons with HIV and their providers should weigh the risks and benefits of attending, versus not attending in-person, HIV-related clinic appointments at this time. Factors to consider include the extent of local COVID-19 transmission, the health needs that will be addressed during the appointment, and the person's HIV status (e.g., CD4 cell count, HIV viral load) and overall health. Virtual visits are an excellent option.
AIDS is the direct complication of infection with HIV.

Opportunistic infection can occur as early as within 12 weeks of antiretroviral treatment. It does not signify treatment failure. Initiate treatment for the opportunistic infection and continue antiretrovirals. In the setting of suboptimal CD4 count, consider modifying therapy. If virologic failure, perform resistance testing and modify therapy.
Refer to Table 1 for the treatment of opportunistic infections.

Patients are usually hospitalized with opportunistic/AIDS-defining illnesses or with diagnosis related to other comorbidities. Patients should be managed according to guidelines for admission, with care paid to medication interactions and social needs. ARV should not be stopped in most hospital settings.

ART should be continued. If the ARV drugs are not on the hospital's formulary, administer medications from the patients' home supplies. Avoid ARV substitution.For patients who are taking an investigational ARV medication as part of their regimen, arrangements should be made with the investigational study team to continue the medication if possible.

For critically ill patients who require tube feeding, some ARV medications are available in liquid formulations and some, but not all, pills may be crushed. Clinicians should consult an HIV specialist and/or pharmacist to assess the best way for a patient with a feeding tube to continue an effective ARV regimenWhen receiving investigational or off-label treatment for COVID-19, please consider interactions with ARV. Persons with HIV should not be excluded from clinical trials for Covid19.

Persons with HIV may need additional assistance with food, mental health services, housing, transportation, and childcare during times of crisis and economic fragility. Clinicians should make every attempt to assess their patients' need for additional social support, at regular intervals. This also includes a heightened awareness for interpersonal violence, and regular assessment,
Data suggests that treated HIV with an undetectable viral load over 3 to 5 years can result in normal lifespan. B
ARV, preventative health and management of complications are fundamental to survival and avoiding hospitalization. C
Monitor plasma HIV-1 RNA levels at 2 and 4 weeks after initiation or change in medication regimen, then every 4 weeks until suppression occurs. C
Assess HIV-1 RNA levels quarterly after confirmed suppression and twice a year after a sustained suppressed viral load for 2 years. C
Primary care can evaluate HIV patients in lieu of HIV specialists with suppressed viral load with annual evaluations from a specialist. C
The natural history of HIV is that it progresses if untreated, to AIDS. The time to progression and the presentation varies with each individual. Refer to the pathophysiology of HIV.
The usual course for treated patients with HIV and AIDS varies with each person.

Elite Controller-is a term applied to a rare group of PLWH who maintain undetectable viral loads in the absence of any treatment. The precise criteria for defining elite controllers often varies from study to study, particularly when it comes to the duration of viral load control.
Long term nonprogressor is an individual with long-term HIV-1 infection who has experienced little or no progressive CD4+ T-cell loss during follow-up. Viral load may be present or minimal.

The best predictor of progression to AIDS and death from AIDS is the plasma viral load (Table 3). When combined with the CD4 cell count, the two markers present a more complete analysis. The plasma viral load correlates linearly with disease progression while the CD4 cell count is inversely related.
Prognostic predictors for the risk of HIV progressing to AIDs are listed in Table 4.

Monitor plasma HIV-1 RNA levels at 2 and 4 weeks after initiation of medication or a change in regimen, then every 4 weeks until suppression occurs. Assess HIV-1 RNA levels quarterly after confirmed suppression. When CD4 cell count are sustained at a level greater than 350/μL and viral load remains suppressed, it is appropriate to evaluate CD4 cell count 6 monthly.12During treatment, there may be intermittent elevations in viral load. However, virologic failure is defined as persistent levels greater than 50 copies/mL. This should prompt the provider to reassess compliance and drug interactions.
Effective therapy is defined as a reduction of HIV-1 RNA at least 10-fold in the first month and, depending on pretreatment viral load, less than 50 copies/mL at 24 weeks.
Resistance testing is recommended in treatment failure while patient is still taking the failed medication.
Screen all pregnant women for HIV and entry into prenatal care and once in the third trimester.
Antiretroviral therapy is recommended for pregnant women to enhance the mother's health and decrease the risk of perinatal transmission.

In general, women living with HIV receiving ARV who present for pregnancy care generally should continue during pregnancy, provided the regimen is tolerated and effective in suppressing viral replication.

Certain drugs should not be continued in pregnant women because of toxicity risk, including stavudine, didanosine, and treatment-dose ritonavir. These drugs should be replaced with ARVs recommended in pregnancy. When feasible, pregnancy in HIV should be managed in collaboration with Maternal fetal medicine along with an infectious disease specialist.

HIV ARV drug-resistance testing should be performed to assist in the selection of active drugs when changing ARV regimens in pregnant women on therapy with virologic failure and HIV RNA levels >1,000 copies/mL. In individuals with HIV RNA levels >500 but <1,000 copies/mL, testing may be unsuccessful but should still be considered.

Due to social, access, behavioral and physical changes in the immediate postpartum period, unique challenges present to ARV adherence, arrangements for new or continued supportive services should be made before hospital discharge.
Contraceptive counseling should start during the prenatal period; a contraceptive plan should be developed prior to hospital discharge.
Women with a positive rapid HIV antibody test during labor require immediate linkage to HIV care and comprehensive follow-up, including confirmation of HIV infection.
Prior to hospital discharge, the woman should be given ARV medications for herself and her newborn to take at home. A

Women may be at increased risk of unintended pregnancy when stay-at-home measures are in effect and continuation or initiation of appropriate contraception should be addressed, including emergency contraception. Based on clinical trial data, use of intrauterine devices and contraceptive implants beyond the expiration date specified on a package insert may be considered. Depot-medroxyprogesterone acetate may also be considered for subcutaneous self-injection..
